pages.summary: Measures of a tone's purity: signal to noise, harmonic distortion, signal to noise and distortion, and the spurious-free dynamic range.
body: Each looks at the spectrum of a signal holding one main tone (through a Kaiser window of beta 38). `snr` gives the tone's power against the noise, with DC and the first n harmonics (6) left out; `thd` the power of harmonics 2 to n against the fundamental's (in dBc, so negative); `sinad` the tone's power against everything else but DC, harmonics included; `sfdr` the tone's power against the largest other component. A tone's power is that of its spectral lobe. `snr(x, y)` is simply 10 log10 of the powers of a signal and its noise.
syntax: With the noise's power, n harmonics left out.
Harmonic distortion, with each harmonic's power and frequency.

examples.title: A tone with a second and third harmonic, in noise

pages.summary: A two-state signal's two levels, and where it crosses midway between them.
body: `statelevels` finds the low and high levels from a histogram of the signal (100 bins): in each half of the range, the average of the samples in its fullest bin. `midcross` gives the times at which each transition crosses the mid-reference level (50% of the way, `'MidPercentReferenceLevel'`), found by linear interpolation; a transition runs from one state's band (`'Tolerance'`, 2% of the levels' difference) to the other's. Times come from fs (the first sample at 0) or the samples' times t. Without outputs, both draw.
syntax: At another reference, with levels given.

examples.title: A clock signal with slow edges

pages.summary: How fast a two-state signal's transitions are.
body: `risetime` gives the time each rising transition takes from the lower reference level to the upper (10% and 90% of the way between the state levels, `'PercentReferenceLevels'`); `falltime` the same for falling transitions; `slewrate` the difference of the reference levels over each transition's duration, negative when falling. The further outputs give the crossing times and the reference levels. Without outputs, each draws.
syntax: [r, lowercross, uppercross, lowerref, upperref] = risetime(x, t, 'PercentReferenceLevels', [lo hi])

examples.title: A trapezoidal pulse

pages.summary: The widths, separations and periods of a two-state signal's pulses, and their duty cycles.
body: A positive pulse rises then falls (`'Polarity'`, `'negative'` for the opposite). Its width runs between its mid-reference crossings; the separation from its end to the next pulse's start; the period from its start to the next one's; the duty cycle is the width over the period. The further outputs give the crossing times. Without outputs, each draws.
syntax: [w, initcross, finalcross, midlev] = pulsewidth(x, t, 'Polarity', p)

examples.title: A pulse train at 30% duty

pages.summary: How a two-state signal's transitions overshoot, undershoot and settle.
body: `overshoot` gives, in percent of the levels' difference, the largest excursion beyond the final state after each transition (within `'SeekFactor'` times the transition's duration after it reaches the state's band; `'Region', 'preshoot'` looks before the transition instead); `undershoot` the excursion back towards the other state; `settlingtime` the time from each mid-reference crossing until the signal stays within `'Tolerance'` percent of its final state, looked for over D after the crossing (NaN when it has not settled by then). The further outputs give the levels and the times. Without outputs, each draws.
syntax: [os, oslev, osinst] = overshoot(x, t, 'Region', r, 'SeekFactor', k)
[s, slev, sinst, tolerance] = settlingtime(x, t, D, 'Tolerance', tol)
